front: What is the management of ASCUS (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance) on Pap smear?
back: If HPV co-test is positive with ASCUS: refer for colposcopy. If HPV co-test is negative with ASCUS: repeat co-test in 1 year (not colposcopy). In women aged 21-24 with ASCUS, repeat cytology in 1 year is preferred over reflexive HPV testing. ASCUS with high-risk HPV positive is managed the same as LSIL.

front: What is the management of LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) on Pap smear?
back: LSIL in women aged 25 and older: colposcopy is preferred. If HPV co-test was done and is negative in women aged 25-29 (which is unusual since HPV isn't routinely co-tested below 30), repeat co-test in 1 year is an option. In women aged 21-24, LSIL is managed with repeat cytology in 1 year because most LSIL regresses spontaneously in this age group. LSIL is associated with HPV infection in more than 75% of cases.

front: What is the management of HSIL (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) on Pap smear?
back: HSIL requires immediate colposcopy with directed biopsy regardless of HPV status. HSIL is associated with CIN 2-3 in about 70-75% of cases and with invasive cancer in 1-2%. If colposcopy is inadequate or biopsy shows CIN 2+, loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) or cold knife conization is performed. Expedited treatment with LEEP without prior biopsy is acceptable in high-risk populations.

front: What are the absolute contraindications to combined estrogen-containing contraceptives?
back: WHO category 4 (never use) absolute contraindications include: migraine with aura, smoker above age 35 (more than 15 cigarettes/day), personal history of VTE, stroke, or CAD, uncontrolled hypertension (above 160/100 mmHg), current or history of breast cancer, liver disease or benign liver tumor, and diabetes with end-organ damage or more than 20 years duration.

front: What are safe contraceptive options for a 38-year-old smoker who has migraines with aura?
back: Estrogen-containing methods are absolutely contraindicated (smoker above 35 AND migraines with aura both independently contraindicate). Safe options include: progestin-only pill (mini-pill), depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA/Depo-Provera), levonorgestrel or etonogestrel subdermal implant (Nexplanon), or hormonal or copper IUD. These methods avoid the stroke risk associated with estrogen.

front: What are the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS and how many criteria are required for diagnosis?
back: PCOS is diagnosed by meeting 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria: (1) oligo-ovulation or anovulation (irregular cycles), (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated free testosterone), and (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (20 or more follicles per ovary using modern high-frequency transvaginal ultrasound, per the 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline, or ovarian volume above 10 mL). Other causes of androgen excess (CAH, Cushing, androgen-secreting tumor) must be excluded.

front: What is the treatment for PCOS in a woman not seeking fertility?
back: Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCP) are first-line for managing irregular cycles and androgen-related symptoms (hirsutism, acne) in PCOS. Spironolactone 50-200 mg/day is added for persistent hirsutism or acne. Metformin 1,500-2,000 mg/day is used when insulin resistance, prediabetes, or obesity is present. Lifestyle modification (diet, weight loss) is cornerstone therapy for all PCOS patients.

front: What is the preferred ovulation induction agent for fertility treatment in PCOS and why?
back: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) 2.5-7.5 mg taken on days 3-7 of the menstrual cycle is preferred over clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction in PCOS. Letrozole achieves higher live birth rates with fewer multiple gestations in PCOS patients. Clomiphene 50-150 mg on days 3-7 is the alternative. Metformin can be added as an adjunct to improve ovulation rates.

front: What are the risk factors for ectopic pregnancy and what is the classic presentation?
back: Risk factors: prior ectopic pregnancy (highest risk), PID or salpingitis, prior tubal surgery (ligation, reversal), assisted reproduction, IUD use (not causative, but if pregnant with IUD, higher ectopic rate), and cigarette smoking. Classic presentation: pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding, and absence of intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound with positive beta-hCG. Ruptured ectopic causes peritoneal signs and hemodynamic instability.

front: What are the criteria for medical (methotrexate) management of ectopic pregnancy?
back: Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM single dose is used for hemodynamically stable ectopic pregnancy with: ectopic mass below 3.5-4 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, beta-hCG below 5,000-10,000 mIU/mL, no severe pain, and no contraindications to MTX (renal, hepatic, or pulmonary disease, immunosuppression). Surgical treatment is required for rupture, hemodynamic instability, or failed MTX therapy.

front: What are the diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia?
back: Preeclampsia requires: new-onset BP at or above 140/90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart after 20 weeks gestation, PLUS proteinuria (at or above 300 mg/24 hours or urine protein-to-creatinine ratio at or above 0.3) OR severe features (BP at or above 160/110, thrombocytopenia below 100,000, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema, or new-onset severe headache).

front: What is the delivery threshold for preeclampsia without severe features and with severe features?
back: Preeclampsia without severe features: delivery at 37 weeks gestation. Preeclampsia with severe features: delivery at 34 weeks (or earlier if maternal or fetal deterioration). Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis during labor and for 24 hours postpartum (dose: 4 g IV loading dose, then 1-2 g/hr maintenance). Antihypertensives (hydralazine IV, labetalol IV, or oral nifedipine) are used when BP is at or above 160/110 mmHg.

front: What is HELLP syndrome and how does it relate to preeclampsia?
back: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) is a severe variant of preeclampsia. Criteria: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (LDH above 600, schistocytes on smear), AST above 70 U/L, and platelets below 100,000/uL. Management includes magnesium sulfate, antihypertensives, and delivery (regardless of gestational age in severe cases). Dexamethasone may temporarily improve platelet count.

front: What is the diagnostic approach for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and what are the glucose targets?
back: Screen all pregnant women for GDM at 24-28 weeks with 1-hour 50 g glucose challenge test (GCT). If GCT is at or above 140 mg/dL (or 130 mg/dL in high-risk), confirm with 3-hour 100 g OGTT. GDM is diagnosed if 2 or more values meet thresholds: fasting at or above 95, 1-hour at or above 180, 2-hour at or above 155, 3-hour at or above 140 mg/dL. Glucose targets: fasting below 95, 1-hour postprandial below 140, 2-hour below 120 mg/dL.

front: What is the treatment approach for gestational diabetes and when is insulin initiated?
back: Start with MNT (medical nutrition therapy) and exercise. If glucose targets are not met within 1-2 weeks (fasting below 95, 1-hr postprandial below 140, 2-hr below 120 mg/dL), initiate insulin. Insulin is preferred over oral agents in pregnancy per ACOG. Metformin may be used as an alternative but crosses the placenta. Adequate glucose control reduces macrosomia, birth trauma, NICU admission, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

front: What is the GBS screening protocol during pregnancy and what is the intrapartum treatment?
back: Screen all pregnant women for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) by vaginal-rectal swab culture at 36-37 weeks gestation. If positive (or unknown status with risk factors), give IV penicillin G 5 million units loading dose, then 2.5-3 million units q4h during labor. Ampicillin is an alternative. Cefazolin is given if penicillin-allergic with low anaphylaxis risk. Clindamycin or vancomycin for high anaphylaxis risk (based on sensitivity).

front: When is RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin) given during pregnancy?
back: Rh-negative mothers who are not sensitized receive RhoGAM 300 mcg IM at 28 weeks gestation (antepartum prophylaxis) and within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive infant. Also given after any sensitizing event: ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, antepartum hemorrhage, or abdominal trauma. Kleihauer-Betke test determines if additional doses are needed after large fetomaternal hemorrhage.

front: What defines menopause and what hormones are used for menopausal symptom management?
back: Menopause is defined as 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea with FSH above 40 mIU/mL and low estradiol, occurring at a median age of 51. Systemic hormone therapy (HT) is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms. Women with an intact uterus require estrogen plus progestogen (to prevent endometrial hyperplasia). Women post-hysterectomy receive estrogen alone. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration.

front: What are the contraindications to menopausal hormone therapy?
back: Absolute contraindications to menopausal HT: unexplained vaginal bleeding, history of breast cancer, history of estrogen-sensitive endometrial cancer, active VTE or high VTE risk, active or recent cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, active liver disease, and history of stroke. Transdermal estrogen has a lower VTE risk than oral estrogen and may be used in women with VTE risk after risk-benefit discussion.

front: What are the BRCA1/2 mutation risk-reduction options for women with confirmed mutations?
back: Women with BRCA1/2 mutations have a lifetime breast cancer risk of 50-85% (BRCA1) and 40-60% (BRCA2). Risk-reduction options: prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) reduces ovarian cancer risk by 80-96% and breast cancer risk when done before natural menopause; prophylactic bilateral mastectomy reduces breast cancer risk by 90-95%; chemoprevention with tamoxifen or raloxifene is less effective but an option for those declining surgery.

front: What is the recommended treatment for uncomplicated chlamydia infection?
back: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days is the preferred treatment for uncomplicated chlamydial urogenital infection (per updated CDC 2021 guidelines, preferred over azithromycin). Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose is an alternative when directly observed therapy is preferred. Test for concurrent gonorrhea and treat if positive. Test of cure at 3 weeks for pharyngeal infection only; retest in 3 months for all patients.

front: What is the recommended treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea infection?
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (or 1 g if weight is at or above 150 kg) is first-line for uncomplicated gonorrhea at all sites (urethral, cervical, rectal, and pharyngeal) per 2021 CDC guidelines. No longer co-treat with azithromycin routinely unless chlamydia co-infection is confirmed or not excluded. Doxycycline 100 mg BID x7 days is added if chlamydia testing is not available.

front: What is the treatment for primary syphilis and how long after treatment should serologic response be assessed?
back: Primary syphilis (painless chancre, positive RPR/VDRL and confirmatory treponemal test) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. In penicillin allergy, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days is the alternative. Check RPR titers at 6 and 12 months; a 4-fold (2 dilution) decrease confirms adequate treatment. Treatment failure or neurosyphilis requires IV penicillin G.

front: What is the treatment for a first episode of genital herpes (HSV)?
back: First episode genital herpes is treated with valacyclovir 1 g twice daily for 7-10 days, or acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 7-10 days. Antiviral therapy reduces duration and severity. Suppressive therapy (valacyclovir 500-1,000 mg daily or acyclovir 400 mg twice daily) is offered for frequent recurrences (at or above 6/year) or to reduce transmission risk to uninfected partners.

front: What is bacterial vaginosis (BV) and what are the Amsel criteria for diagnosis?
back: BV is a dysbiosis of vaginal flora with loss of Lactobacillus and overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes. Amsel criteria (3 of 4 required): thin, grey-white homogeneous discharge; vaginal pH above 4.5; positive whiff test (fishy odor with KOH); and clue cells on wet prep (above 20% of epithelial cells). Treatment: metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days or 0.75% gel intravaginal once daily for 5 days.

front: What is the treatment for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (3 or more episodes per year)?
back: Recurrent VVC (at or above 3 episodes/year) is treated with an induction phase: fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses, followed by maintenance therapy: weekly fluconazole 150 mg for 6 months. This suppressive regimen reduces recurrence in about 90% of women. Evaluate for underlying diabetes, HIV, or immunosuppression. Oral fluconazole is preferred over topical azoles for systemic suppression.

front: What are the diagnostic criteria and treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
back: PID clinical criteria: uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness in a sexually active woman without other clear cause. Empiric treatment should be started. Outpatient regimen: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once PLUS doxycycline 100 mg BID x14 days WITH metronidazole 500 mg BID x14 days. Inpatient criteria: TOA, pregnancy, severe illness, inability to tolerate oral, or failure of outpatient treatment.

front: What are the emergency contraception options and their effective time windows?
back: Copper IUD (Paragard): most effective emergency contraception, reduces pregnancy risk by above 99%, effective up to 5 days after unprotected sex. Ella (ulipristal acetate) 30 mg: effective up to 120 hours (5 days). Plan B (levonorgestrel) 1.5 mg: effective up to 72 hours but can be used up to 120 hours with reduced efficacy. BMI above 30 kg/m2 reduces levonorgestrel EC efficacy; copper IUD or ella preferred in obese patients.

front: What are the most common causes of postmenopausal bleeding and what is the evaluation?
back: Any postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) must be evaluated to exclude endometrial cancer (most concerning cause). Common causes: endometrial atrophy (most common), endometrial polyp, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial carcinoma. Evaluation: transvaginal ultrasound (endometrial stripe below 4-5 mm makes cancer less likely) followed by endometrial biopsy if stripe is above 4 mm, bleeding persists, or high-risk features are present.

front: What are the risk factors for endometrial cancer and how does it present?
back: Risk factors: unopposed estrogen exposure (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen use, estrogen-only HT, anovulation), late menopause, nulliparity, diabetes, and hereditary syndromes (Lynch syndrome). Endometrial cancer presents with postmenopausal bleeding (most common) or abnormal uterine bleeding in premenopausal women. Endometrial biopsy is the primary diagnostic test; D&C under hysteroscopy is used when biopsy is insufficient.

front: What is the intrauterine device (IUD) selection guide for different clinical scenarios?
back: Copper IUD (Paragard): non-hormonal, preferred for women who want to avoid hormones, lasts up to 10-12 years, most effective EC; may worsen dysmenorrhea. Levonorgestrel IUDs (Mirena 52 mg: 8 years; Kyleena 19.5 mg: 5 years; Skyla 13.5 mg: 3 years): reduce menstrual bleeding and cramping, preferred in endometriosis or heavy menstrual bleeding. Both are safe in nulliparous women and do not affect future fertility.

front: What are the common causes and treatment of dysmenorrhea?
back: Primary dysmenorrhea: painful menses without pelvic pathology, due to excess prostaglandins. Treat with NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800 mg or naproxen 500 mg TID, starting 1-2 days before onset and continuing through day 2-3). Combined OCP reduces prostaglandin production. Secondary dysmenorrhea: due to endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis, or PID. Laparoscopy may be needed to diagnose endometriosis.

front: What is endometriosis and what are the first-line pharmacologic treatments?
back: Endometriosis is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, causing dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, and subfertility. First-line hormonal treatments: combined OCP (cyclic or continuous), progestin-only methods (norethindrone acetate, DMPA, LNG-IUD), and NSAIDs for pain. Second-line: GnRH agonists (leuprolide depot) with add-back hormone therapy. Definitive diagnosis is by laparoscopy with biopsy.

front: What is the workup for secondary amenorrhea?
back: Secondary amenorrhea (absence of menses for 3 months in previously regular cycles or 6 months in irregular) requires: pregnancy test first (always), then TSH, prolactin, FSH, and LH. High FSH: premature ovarian insufficiency. Low FSH/LH: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (hypothalamic amenorrhea, pituitary pathology). High prolactin: pituitary adenoma (MRI brain). Progesterone challenge test assesses estrogen status and outflow tract.

front: What is premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and how is it distinguished from menopause?
back: POI (formerly premature menopause) is loss of ovarian function before age 40, defined by FSH above 40 mIU/mL on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart with amenorrhea for at least 4 months. Unlike menopause, POI may have intermittent ovarian function and spontaneous pregnancy is possible (5-10%). Causes: autoimmune (most common), Turner syndrome, fragile X premutation, and iatrogenic. Hormone replacement until age 50 is recommended to prevent osteoporosis and cardiovascular effects.

front: What is the USPSTF recommendation for ovarian cancer screening?
back: USPSTF recommends against routine screening for ovarian cancer in average-risk women (D recommendation). Transvaginal ultrasound and CA-125 testing do not reduce mortality and lead to false positives with unnecessary surgery. Women with BRCA1/2 mutations, Lynch syndrome, or strong family history of ovarian cancer should be referred to genetic counseling and high-risk surveillance programs.

front: What are the USPSTF screening recommendations for domestic violence/intimate partner violence?
back: USPSTF recommends screening all women of reproductive age (14-46) for intimate partner violence (IPV) and referring those who screen positive to ongoing support services. Validated screening tools include HITS (Hurt, Insult, Threaten, Scream) and WAST (Woman Abuse Screening Tool). Screen in a private setting without the partner present. Document findings using the patient's own words.

front: What is vulvodynia and what are the treatment options?
back: Vulvodynia is chronic vulvar pain lasting at least 3 months without an identifiable cause (not caused by infection, inflammation, or skin disease). Provoked vestibulodynia (pain with touch or insertion) is the most common type. Treatments include topical lidocaine 2% gel or ointment, topical amitriptyline/baclofen creams, oral tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline 10-75 mg), gabapentin 300-1,800 mg/day, pelvic floor physical therapy, and vestibulectomy for refractory cases.

front: What is the treatment for postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) and what are the most common causes?
back: The 4 Ts of PPH causes: Tone (uterine atony, most common cause of 80%), Trauma (lacerations, uterine rupture), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes), Thrombin (coagulopathy). Treatment of uterine atony: uterine massage, oxytocin 10-40 units IV infusion, methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM (avoid in HTN), carboprost (Hemabate) 0.25 mg IM, misoprostol 600-1,000 mcg PR/SL. Bimanual compression and surgical intervention if bleeding continues.

front: What are the indications for cervical cerclage during pregnancy?
back: Cervical cerclage is a surgical procedure placing a stitch around the cervix to prevent preterm birth. Indications: (1) history-indicated: at least 3 prior second-trimester losses or preterm deliveries, placed at 12-14 weeks; (2) ultrasound-indicated: cervical length below 25 mm before 24 weeks in a patient with prior preterm birth; (3) physical exam-indicated (emergency): dilated cervix with membranes visible. Progesterone supplementation is also used for cervical shortening.

front: What is the recommended prenatal lab panel at the first obstetric visit?
back: First prenatal visit labs: blood type and Rh factor, antibody screen, CBC, rubella IgG titer, varicella immunity, hepatitis B surface antigen, syphilis (RPR or VDRL), HIV (opt-out testing), gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT, urinalysis and urine culture, Pap smear (if due), TSH (if symptomatic or high risk), and hemoglobin electrophoresis (if at risk for hemoglobinopathy). Genetic carrier screening is offered to all patients.

front: What supplements are recommended for pregnant women and in what doses?
back: Folic acid 400-800 mcg daily beginning at least 1 month before conception and through the first trimester reduces neural tube defects by 50-70%. High-risk women (prior NTD, on antiepileptic drugs) need 4,000 mcg (4 mg) daily. Iron 27 mg/day elemental iron. Calcium 1,000 mg/day. Iodine 150-220 mcg/day. Omega-3 DHA 200-300 mg/day. Avoid vitamin A above 10,000 IU (teratogenic in excess).

front: What are the indications for elective cesarean delivery and what are the key risks?
back: Indications for C-section: prior classical (vertical) uterine incision (VBAC contraindicated), active genital herpes at labor onset, certain placenta previa or accreta spectrum disorders, malpresentation at term, and certain maternal cardiac or neurologic conditions. C-section risks include increased bleeding, infection, injury to adjacent organs, thromboembolism, and future placenta accreta risk. VBAC success rate is 60-80% in appropriate candidates.

front: What is placenta previa and how is it managed?
back: Placenta previa is placental implantation over or adjacent to the internal cervical os, presenting with painless bright red vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester. Diagnosed by transvaginal ultrasound. Management: pelvic rest (no vaginal exams, intercourse, or tampons), hospitalization if bleeding is significant, antenatal corticosteroids if below 34 weeks, and planned C-section at 36-37 weeks. Avoid digital cervical examination.

front: What is placental abruption and how does it differ from placenta previa?
back: Placental abruption is premature separation of the normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall, causing painful vaginal bleeding and uterine rigidity (board-like abdomen). Risk factors: hypertension, cocaine use, trauma, prior abruption. Unlike placenta previa (painless bleeding), abruption is painful. Severe abruption causes DIC and fetal distress. Management depends on gestational age and severity; may require emergency delivery.

front: What is postpartum depression and how does it differ from postpartum blues?
back: Postpartum blues (baby blues): transient mood lability, tearfulness, anxiety lasting 2-3 days to 2 weeks postpartum; affects 50-80% of women; resolves spontaneously. Postpartum depression (PPD): major depressive episode occurring within 4 weeks to 1 year postpartum; affects 10-15% of women; requires treatment. Screen with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS); score at or above 13 indicates PPD. First-line treatment: sertraline (preferred as minimal breast milk transfer) or psychotherapy.

front: What are the USPSTF recommendations for breast cancer prevention with chemoprevention?
back: USPSTF recommends clinicians offer risk-reducing medications to women at increased breast cancer risk (5-year risk at or above 3% by Tyrer-Cuzick or similar model) after risk-benefit discussion. Options: tamoxifen 20 mg/day x5 years (premenopausal or postmenopausal), raloxifene 60 mg/day x5 years (postmenopausal only), or exemestane 25 mg/day x5 years (postmenopausal). These reduce risk by 30-50% but have side effects including VTE and hot flashes.

front: What are the characteristics and management of gestational hypertension?
back: Gestational hypertension: BP at or above 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks gestation without proteinuria or other severe features. It resolves by 12 weeks postpartum. Monitor weekly for development of preeclampsia features. Antihypertensives are started if BP is at or above 160/110 mmHg (labetalol or nifedipine oral). Deliver at 37 weeks. Gestational HTN resolving postpartum does not require long-term antihypertensive therapy.

front: What STI screening is recommended for all sexually active women under 25 per USPSTF?
back: USPSTF recommends annual chlamydia and gonorrhea screening for all sexually active women aged 24 and younger, and for older women who are at increased risk (new or multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, prior STI, commercial sex work). Syphilis screening is recommended for women at high risk. HIV testing is recommended at least once for all adults aged 15-65, and more frequently for high-risk individuals.

front: What is the difference between primary and secondary dyspareunia?
back: Primary dyspareunia: painful intercourse since first attempt at penetration. Secondary dyspareunia: pain develops after a period of pain-free intercourse. Common causes by location: superficial/entry dyspareunia (vulvodynia, vaginismus, skin conditions); deep dyspareunia (endometriosis, PID, ovarian cysts, uterine fibroids). Evaluation includes pelvic exam, culture, hormonal assessment, and imaging. Treatment targets underlying etiology.

front: What is vaginismus and how is it treated?
back: Vaginismus (now termed genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder) is involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor muscles preventing vaginal penetration, causing pain or inability to complete intercourse. Treatment includes pelvic floor physical therapy with progressive vaginal dilator therapy, psychosexual therapy or CBT, and topical lidocaine for pain relief. Botulinum toxin injection into the pubococcygeus muscle is an option for refractory cases.

front: What is the recommended screening for ovarian cancer in women with BRCA mutations?
back: Women with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations do not have a proven effective screening method for ovarian cancer. USPSTF, ACOG, and NCCN acknowledge no survival benefit for transvaginal ultrasound or CA-125 screening. Prophylactic bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) at age 35-40 (BRCA1) or 40-45 (BRCA2) after completion of childbearing is recommended as the most effective risk-reduction strategy.

front: What is the normal CA-125 level and when is it used clinically?
back: Normal CA-125 is below 35 U/mL. It is used to monitor response to treatment in known ovarian cancer, not for primary screening. It can be elevated in benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, PID, liver disease, menstruation) reducing its specificity. ROMA score (combining CA-125 and HE4) is used preoperatively to assess malignancy risk in women with pelvic masses before surgical planning.

front: What are the effects of the progestin-only pill (mini-pill) and what is the main concern with missing a dose?
back: The progestin-only pill (norethindrone 0.35 mg daily) works primarily by thickening cervical mucus and suppressing ovulation in about 50% of cycles. It must be taken at the same time daily (within 3-hour window). If more than 3 hours late, use backup contraception for 48 hours. It is safe for breastfeeding women and those with estrogen contraindications. The newer norethindrone 0.075 mg pill (Slynd) has a 24-hour missed-pill window.

front: What is depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) and what are its advantages and disadvantages?
back: DMPA (Depo-Provera) 150 mg IM every 12-13 weeks (approximately every 3 months) or subcutaneous 104 mg every 12-13 weeks is a highly effective progestin-only contraceptive (failure rate below 1% with perfect use). Advantages: no daily pill, good for women who cannot use estrogen, reduces sickle cell crises. Disadvantages: bone mineral density loss (reversible after stopping), irregular bleeding or amenorrhea, weight gain, and delayed return of fertility (median 10 months after last injection).

front: What is the BRCA gene testing indication and referral criteria?
back: Refer for BRCA genetic counseling and testing when: personal history of breast cancer below age 50, bilateral breast cancer, triple-negative breast cancer below 60, breast and ovarian cancer in same patient, male breast cancer, two first-degree relatives with breast or ovarian cancer, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry with family breast/ovarian cancer history, or family member with known BRCA mutation. USPSTF recommends risk assessment tool (Ontario BRCA or equivalent) before referral.

front: What is the recommended timing and type of fetal surveillance in a post-term pregnancy?
back: Post-term pregnancy is beyond 42 weeks (41 0/7 to 42 6/7 weeks is late-term). ACOG recommends initiating fetal surveillance (non-stress test twice weekly or biophysical profile) starting at 41 weeks and offering membrane sweeping at 39-40 weeks. Induction of labor is offered at 41 weeks to reduce risks of meconium aspiration, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, placental insufficiency, and stillbirth. Cervical ripening with prostaglandins or mechanical methods may be needed.

front: What is the first-line treatment for urge urinary incontinence in women?
back: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises) and bladder training are first-line non-pharmacologic treatments. First-line pharmacotherapy: antimuscarinics (oxybutynin extended-release 5-30 mg daily, solifenacin 5-10 mg daily, tolterodine ER 4 mg daily). Beta-3 agonist mirabegron 25-50 mg daily is equally effective with fewer anticholinergic effects (preferred in older adults to avoid cognitive side effects). Combination oxybutynin + mirabegron is more effective than monotherapy.

front: What is stress urinary incontinence and what are the treatment options?
back: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is leakage of urine with increased intraabdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, laughing, exercise). Caused by urethral hypermobility or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. First-line: pelvic floor physical therapy (Kegel exercises), pessary for urethral support. Topical vaginal estrogen if atrophic vaginitis is present. Surgical options: midurethral sling (synthetic mesh) is most effective. No FDA-approved pharmacotherapy specifically for SUI in the US.

front: What are the antenatal corticosteroid indications and regimen during preterm labor?
back: Antenatal corticosteroids are given to women at risk for preterm delivery between 24 0/7 and 34 6/7 weeks gestation. Regimen: betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses. Benefits: reduces RDS, IVH, NEC, and neonatal death. A single rescue course may be considered if prior course was given more than 14 days ago and delivery remains imminent at less than 34 weeks.

front: What is the recommended antibiotic prophylaxis for Cesarean section and when should it be given?
back: Cefazolin is the preferred prophylactic antibiotic for C-section, given as a single IV dose within 60 minutes before skin incision. Dosing: 2 g IV (or 3 g IV if weight is at or above 120 kg). Azithromycin 500 mg IV may be added for unscheduled C-sections after labor or rupture of membranes to reduce endometritis. Clindamycin plus gentamicin is used in penicillin-allergic patients.

front: What is the ACOG recommendation for folic acid supplementation to prevent neural tube defects?
back: All women capable of becoming pregnant should take 400-800 mcg of folic acid daily. Women with a prior NTD-affected pregnancy or on valproate, carbamazepine, or methotrexate should take 4,000 mcg (4 mg) daily beginning 1-3 months before conception. Folic acid supplementation reduces NTD risk by 50-70%. NTDs occur in the first 28 days post-conception, often before women know they are pregnant.

front: What is the clinical management of a spontaneous abortion (miscarriage) in the first trimester?
back: Options for complete management of first trimester miscarriage: (1) Expectant management (natural expulsion) within 2-6 weeks; (2) Medical management: misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally or sublingually (85-90% complete within 1 week); (3) Surgical management: manual or electric vacuum aspiration, most rapid and definitive. Rh-negative patients should receive RhoGAM. Emotional support and follow-up beta-hCG to confirm completion are essential.

front: What are the key differences between primary and secondary infertility workup?
back: Primary infertility: no prior pregnancies. Secondary infertility: inability to conceive after a prior pregnancy. Workup is similar for both: semen analysis (male factor accounts for 30-40% of infertility), ovarian reserve testing (AMH, day 3 FSH and estradiol, antral follicle count), hysterosalpingography (HSG) to assess tubal patency and uterine cavity, and evaluation of ovulation (day 21 progesterone, LH surge monitoring). Investigate after 12 months of unprotected sex (6 months if above age 35).

front: What is the recommended timing for a follow-up Pap smear after treatment for CIN 2 or CIN 3?
back: After treatment for CIN 2 or CIN 3 (LEEP, cold knife cone, or cryotherapy), patients require surveillance co-testing (Pap plus HPV) at 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months. If all three are negative, return to routine co-testing every 3 years for 25 years (total). Persistent positive HPV with any abnormal cytology requires colposcopy. CIN 2/3 recurrence rates are 5-10% within 2 years of treatment.

front: What is lichen sclerosus and how is it treated?
back: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis most commonly affecting the vulva in postmenopausal women (but can occur in any age or sex). Presents with white, crinkled, atrophic skin, severe pruritus, and dyspareunia. Thin, fragile skin may fuse the labia minora or clitoral hood. First-line treatment: ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment) daily for 3 months, then tapered to 2-3x/week for maintenance. Biopsy if suspicious for malignancy.

front: What is the USPSTF recommendation for STI counseling for sexually active adolescents and adults?
back: USPSTF recommends intensive behavioral counseling for all sexually active adolescents and for adults at increased risk for STIs (multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, prior STI, illicit drug use). Counseling covers condom use, risk reduction, STI testing, and partner notification. High-intensity interventions (multiple sessions, individualized) reduce STI incidence. Brief counseling at every visit is also recommended.

front: What is trichomonas vaginalis infection and how is it treated?
back: Trichomonas vaginalis is the most common curable STI worldwide. Presentation: profuse, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge with a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate hemorrhages) and vaginal pH above 4.5. Motile trichomonads on wet prep confirm diagnosis; NAAT is more sensitive. Treatment is sex-specific per CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: women receive metronidazole 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days (preferred, higher cure rate in women), while men receive metronidazole 2 g PO single dose. Tinidazole 2 g PO single dose is an alternative. Treat partners concurrently. Test-of-cure at 2-3 weeks is recommended due to reinfection and treatment failure risk.

front: What is the management of a woman found to have HPV 16 or 18 on co-testing with a negative Pap smear?
back: HPV 16 and 18 are the highest-risk genotypes, responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancers. Per ASCCP 2019 guidelines, women with HPV 16 or 18 detected on co-testing (even with negative cytology) should proceed directly to colposcopy rather than returning for repeat co-testing in 1 year. This differs from 'other high-risk HPV' genotypes (not 16/18) with negative cytology, which can be repeated in 1 year.

front: What are the USPSTF recommendations for breast cancer screening with mammography?
back: The finalized 2024 USPSTF recommendation calls for biennial mammography starting at age 40 for all average-risk women (B recommendation), replacing the older 2016 stance that started routine screening at 50. Women with high-risk factors such as BRCA mutations may need earlier or more frequent screening.

front: What does postmenopausal bleeding always require in clinical evaluation?
back: Postmenopausal bleeding always requires endometrial biopsy to rule out endometrial cancer. Any vaginal bleeding occurring more than 12 months after the last menstrual period is considered postmenopausal. Transvaginal ultrasound showing endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm also warrants biopsy.

front: Which HPV strains cause most cervical cancers, and what is the recommended vaccination age range?
back: HPV types 16 and 18 cause approximately 70% of all cervical cancers. The HPV vaccine is routinely recommended for individuals ages 9-26. For adults ages 27-45, shared decision-making is used, as benefit decreases with age and prior HPV exposure.

front: What is the most common type of uterine fibroid, and what medical treatments are available for heavy bleeding?
back: Intramural fibroids are the most common type of uterine fibroid, located within the muscular wall of the uterus. Medical treatments for heavy uterine bleeding include progestin-releasing IUDs (such as levonorgestrel IUD), combined oral contraceptives, and GnRH agonists such as leuprolide. Surgical options include myomectomy or hysterectomy.

front: What are the classic symptoms of endometriosis and how is it definitively diagnosed?
back: Endometriosis presents with cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea (painful periods), dyspareunia (painful intercourse), and infertility. First-line medical treatment includes combined oral contraceptives or progestins. Definitive diagnosis requires laparoscopy with direct visualization and biopsy of endometrial tissue outside the uterus.

front: What are the four main types of endometriosis lesions and which location causes the most severe symptoms?
back: The four types of endometriosis lesions are peritoneal implants, ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts), deep infiltrating endometriosis, and rectovaginal nodules. Deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the rectovaginal septum tends to cause the most severe pain, including dyschezia (painful bowel movements). Ovarian endometriomas greater than 4 cm are typically managed surgically.

front: What is the ASCCP guideline for managing a patient with LSIL on Pap smear who is 25 years old?
back: For a patient age 25 or older with LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), colposcopy is recommended. For patients ages 21-24, a 12-month repeat Pap smear is preferred over immediate colposcopy, as most LSIL in this age group regresses spontaneously. HPV co-testing guides further management in women 30 and older.

front: What is the standard treatment for bacterial vaginosis, and how does it differ in pregnant patients?
back: Bacterial vaginosis is treated with metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, or metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel once daily for 5 days, or clindamycin 2% vaginal cream at bedtime for 7 days. In pregnant patients, oral metronidazole is preferred as intravaginal clindamycin cream has been associated with preterm birth. All symptomatic pregnant women with BV should be treated.

front: What are the diagnostic criteria and first-line treatment for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?
back: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, requiring 2 of 3 features: oligomenorrhea or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (elevated free testosterone, hirsutism, acne), and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (20 or more follicles in one ovary (per the 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline) or ovarian volume over 10 mL). First-line treatment is combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation and hirsutism, plus metformin for insulin resistance and metabolic concerns.

front: What are the contraindications to combined oral contraceptive use (COCP)?
back: Absolute contraindications to COCPs include age 35 or older plus smoking 15 or more cigarettes per day, uncontrolled hypertension (systolic above 160 or diastolic above 100), personal history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, migraine with aura at any age, history of breast cancer, and active liver disease. Women with migraine with aura have a 2-fold increased stroke risk with estrogen-containing contraceptives.

front: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD)?
back: MDD requires 5 or more of 9 SIGECAPS symptoms present for at least 2 weeks, and must include either depressed mood or anhedonia (loss of interest). SIGECAPS stands for Sleep changes, Interest loss, Guilt, Energy loss, Concentration problems, Appetite changes, Psychomotor changes, and Suicidal ideation. Symptoms must cause significant impairment and not be caused by substances or another medical condition.

front: What are the DSM-5 criteria for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)?
back: GAD requires excessive, uncontrollable worry occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, accompanied by at least 3 of 6 symptoms: restlessness, easy fatigability, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance. First-line treatment is an SSRI or SNRI combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Common first-line SSRIs include sertraline (50-200 mg) and escitalopram (10-20 mg).

front: What distinguishes Bipolar I from Bipolar II disorder?
back: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode lasting 7 or more days (or of any duration if hospitalization is required). Bipolar II disorder is characterized by at least one hypomanic episode (lasting 4 or more days, less severe than mania) plus at least one major depressive episode, with no history of full mania. First-line mood stabilizers for Bipolar I include lithium and valproate; lamotrigine is preferred for the depressive phase of Bipolar II.

front: What are the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, and what is the first-line treatment for a first episode?
back: Schizophrenia requires 2 or more of the following for at least 1 month: hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, alogia). Total duration including prodrome must be at least 6 months. For a first episode, second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) such as risperidone or aripiprazole are first-line due to a more favorable side effect profile than first-generation agents.

front: What are the DSM-5 criteria for PTSD, and which medications are FDA-approved for its treatment?
back: PTSD requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, followed by symptoms in four clusters lasting more than 1 month: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative alterations in cognition or mood, and alterations in arousal or reactivity. The only two FDA-approved medications for PTSD are sertraline (Zoloft) and paroxetine (Paxil), both SSRIs. Trauma-focused CBT is the gold-standard psychotherapy.

front: What is the first-line treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)?
back: First-line treatment for OCD is exposure and response prevention (ERP) therapy combined with an SSRI. SSRIs for OCD typically require higher doses than for depression, such as fluoxetine 40-80 mg, sertraline 100-200 mg, or fluvoxamine 100-300 mg. Response may take 8-12 weeks. For treatment-resistant OCD, augmentation with low-dose antipsychotics such as risperidone may be added.

front: What are the diagnostic criteria for panic disorder, and what is the recommended first-line treatment?
back: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus at least 1 month of persistent concern about future attacks, their consequences, or significant behavioral change to avoid them. First-line treatment is an SSRI (such as sertraline 25-200 mg or escitalopram 10-20 mg) combined with CBT. Long-term benzodiazepine use should be avoided due to dependence risk, though they may be used short-term for acute symptom relief.

front: What is the first-line treatment for ADHD in children under age 6 versus children age 6 and older?
back: For children under age 6 with ADHD, behavioral therapy alone is the first-line treatment, as the risks of stimulant medications outweigh benefits in very young children. For children age 6 and older, both behavioral therapy and stimulant medications are first-line, with methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) and amphetamine salts (Adderall) being the most commonly used agents. Starting doses of methylphenidate are typically 5 mg twice daily.

front: What are the first-line pharmacologic options for ADHD in adults?
back: First-line pharmacologic treatment for adult ADHD includes stimulants: mixed amphetamine salts (Adderall, starting at 5-10 mg daily) and methylphenidate formulations (Concerta, Ritalin, starting at 18-36 mg daily). Atomoxetine (Strattera), a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is the primary non-stimulant option and preferred when there is a history of substance use disorder or significant anxiety. Bupropion and viloxazine are additional non-stimulant alternatives.

front: What is the therapeutic lithium level, and what signs indicate toxicity?
back: The therapeutic lithium level for maintenance is 0.6-1.2 mEq/L (acute mania 0.8-1.2 mEq/L). Mild-to-moderate toxicity occurs at levels above 1.5 mEq/L and presents with tremor, diarrhea, nausea, and confusion. Severe toxicity occurs above 2.0 mEq/L with seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and can be life-threatening. TSH, BMP (renal function), and lithium levels should be monitored every 6-12 months in stable patients.

front: What serious adverse effect is associated with clozapine, and how is it monitored?
back: Clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis, a potentially fatal reduction in white blood cells that occurs in approximately 1% of patients. Because of this risk, clozapine requires enrollment in the REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy) program with mandatory absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring weekly for 6 months, then every 2 weeks for 6 months, and then monthly thereafter. Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

front: What is tardive dyskinesia, what causes it, and how is it treated?
back: Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is an involuntary movement disorder characterized by repetitive, purposeless movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, choreiform limb movements) caused by long-term use of dopamine receptor antagonists, particularly first-generation antipsychotics. FDA-approved treatments include valbenazine (Ingrezza, 40-80 mg daily) and deutetrabenazine (Austedo, 12-48 mg daily), both of which are VMAT2 inhibitors that reduce dopamine release.

front: What are the extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) of antipsychotics and how are they managed?
back: EPS from antipsychotics include akathisia (subjective restlessness), acute dystonia (painful involuntary muscle spasm), and pseudoparkinsonism (rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor). Acute dystonia is treated with benztropine 1-2 mg IM or IV, or diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IM. Akathisia responds best to propranolol 20-40 mg or mirtazapine. Pseudoparkinsonism is managed with benztropine or amantadine, or by switching to a lower-potency antipsychotic.

front: What is serotonin syndrome and which drug combinations commonly cause it?
back: Serotonin syndrome is characterized by a clinical triad of mental status changes (agitation, confusion), autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension), and neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor). Common causative combinations include SSRIs with tramadol, fentanyl, triptans, linezolid, or MAOIs. Onset is typically rapid, within hours of exposure. Clonus is the hallmark neuromuscular finding.

front: How does neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) differ from serotonin syndrome?
back: NMS is caused by dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) and presents with lead-pipe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and autonomic instability, typically developing over days. Serotonin syndrome is caused by serotonergic drugs and presents with clonus, hyperreflexia, and develops within hours. NMS does not produce clonus. Treatment for NMS includes stopping the offending agent, dantrolene (a muscle relaxant), and bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist); ICU admission is often required.

front: What is the CIWA-Ar scale used for, and what scores guide management of alcohol withdrawal?
back: The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) measures severity of alcohol withdrawal using 10 items including tremor, diaphoresis, anxiety, agitation, and perceptual disturbances. A score of 8-14 indicates moderate withdrawal warranting medication. A score of 15 or more indicates severe withdrawal requiring inpatient management. Benzodiazepines are first-line pharmacotherapy, with lorazepam preferred in liver disease and diazepam used for longer-acting coverage.

front: What does a positive CAGE questionnaire indicate?
back: The CAGE questionnaire screens for alcohol use disorder with four questions: Have you felt you should Cut down? Have people Annoyed you by criticizing your drinking? Have you felt Guilty about drinking? Have you had an Eye-opener drink in the morning? A score of 2 or more positive responses indicates likely alcohol use disorder and warrants further evaluation. Sensitivity is approximately 71-85% for AUD.

front: What is buprenorphine, how does it work, and when should it be initiated?
back: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa-opioid antagonist used for opioid use disorder (OUD). It should be initiated when the patient has a Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 8-12 or greater, indicating mild-to-moderate withdrawal, to prevent precipitating severe withdrawal. It is given sublingually (Suboxone combines buprenorphine with naloxone). Typical starting dose is 2-4 mg sublingually, titrating to 8-24 mg daily.

front: What is naltrexone, and what precautions are needed before starting it for opioid use disorder?
back: Naltrexone is a full opioid receptor antagonist used for both opioid use disorder and alcohol use disorder (AUD). Before initiating naltrexone for OUD, the patient must be completely opioid-free for at least 7-10 days (10-14 days for methadone) to avoid precipitating severe withdrawal. Naloxone challenge testing may be done before the first dose. Monthly injectable naltrexone (Vivitrol 380 mg IM) improves adherence over oral formulations.

front: What is acamprosate and what makes it unique among alcohol use disorder medications?
back: Acamprosate (Campral) reduces alcohol cravings by modulating glutamate and GABA neurotransmitter systems in patients who have already achieved abstinence. A key advantage is that it is safe to use in patients with liver disease, as it is renally cleared rather than hepatically metabolized. The standard dose is 666 mg (two 333 mg tablets) three times daily, for a total of 6 tablets per day (1,998 mg/day total). It does not prevent intoxication if the patient drinks.

front: How does disulfiram work for alcohol use disorder, and what is the most important patient education point?
back: Disulfiram (Antabuse) inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, the enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde, a toxic byproduct of alcohol metabolism. If alcohol is consumed while taking disulfiram, acetaldehyde accumulates causing flushing, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and tachycardia. The most critical patient education point is that the patient must maintain complete abstinence from all alcohol-containing products, including mouthwash, sauces, and topical preparations, as even small amounts trigger the reaction.

front: What combination of factors defines high suicide risk, and what is the key intervention strategy?
back: High suicide risk is defined by the presence of a specific plan (how), access to means (what), and stated intent (when/will do it), requiring inpatient psychiatric admission. Lethal means counseling and means restriction is the single most evidence-based intervention, particularly securing or removing firearms from the home, which are involved in approximately 50% of suicide deaths in the US. Safety planning is an essential outpatient tool.

front: What is the PHQ-9, and what scores correlate with MDD severity?
back: The PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9) is a validated 9-item depression screening and severity tool based on the DSM criteria for MDD, with each item scored 0-3. Scores of 5-9 indicate mild depression, 10-14 indicate moderate depression, 15-19 indicate moderately severe depression, and 20-27 indicate severe depression. A score of 10 or above is the standard threshold for initiating treatment.

front: What are the first-line SSRIs for depression and their typical starting and target doses?
back: Common first-line SSRIs for MDD include sertraline (start 25-50 mg, target 50-200 mg daily), escitalopram (start 5-10 mg, target 10-20 mg daily), and fluoxetine (start 10-20 mg, target 20-60 mg daily). An adequate trial requires at least 4-8 weeks at a therapeutic dose before declaring treatment failure. Sertraline and escitalopram have the most favorable drug interaction profiles.

front: What is the mechanism and clinical use of venlafaxine, and when is it preferred over SSRIs?
back: Venlafaxine (Effexor) is an SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) that inhibits both serotonin and norepinephrine transporters. It is preferred when a patient has comorbid anxiety and depression, neuropathic pain, or fibromyalgia. Target doses for depression are 75-225 mg daily. At doses below 150 mg, it acts predominantly as an SSRI; norepinephrine reuptake inhibition becomes clinically significant at 150 mg and above.

front: What are the unique properties of bupropion (Wellbutrin) that distinguish it from SSRIs?
back: Bupropion inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake and has no serotonergic activity. It does not cause sexual dysfunction or weight gain, making it preferred when these SSRI side effects are a concern. It is also FDA-approved for smoking cessation (Zyban) at 150 mg twice daily. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in patients with eating disorders (bulimia, anorexia), seizure disorders, and abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

front: What is mirtazapine and when is it particularly useful in depression management?
back: Mirtazapine (Remeron) is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA) that blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and histamine receptors. It is particularly useful in patients with depression complicated by insomnia, poor appetite, or significant weight loss, as it promotes sedation and weight gain. Standard dosing is 15-45 mg at bedtime. Paradoxically, lower doses (7.5-15 mg) are more sedating than higher doses.

front: What is the black box warning for SSRIs in children and young adults?
back: SSRIs carry an FDA black box warning for increased risk of suicidal ideation and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults up to age 24. This risk is highest in the first 1-4 weeks of treatment. All patients started on SSRIs should be seen within 1-2 weeks of initiation, and more frequently in pediatric and young adult patients. The absolute risk increase is small (4% vs 2% placebo), and untreated depression carries a higher overall suicide risk.

front: What is the clinical presentation and treatment of social anxiety disorder?
back: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) presents with marked fear or anxiety about social situations where the individual may be scrutinized, lasting 6 or more months and causing significant functional impairment. First-line treatment is CBT (specifically, exposure-based therapy) and SSRIs, with paroxetine, sertraline, and fluvoxamine CR all FDA-approved. Beta-blockers such as propranolol 10-40 mg can be used situationally for performance anxiety but are not effective for generalized social anxiety.

front: What are the DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder (AUD) and how is severity classified?
back: AUD is diagnosed when 2 or more of 11 criteria are met within a 12-month period, including tolerance, withdrawal, using more than intended, failed attempts to cut down, time spent obtaining/using/recovering, craving, role failure, interpersonal problems, giving up activities, hazardous use, and continued use despite knowledge of harm. Mild AUD = 2-3 criteria, moderate = 4-5 criteria, severe = 6 or more criteria.

front: What are the signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal and how is severity assessed?
back: Opioid withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, restlessness, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, diaphoresis, piloerection (goosebumps), nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle aches, and insomnia. The Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scores 11 items on a 0-48 scale: scores 5-12 = mild, 13-24 = moderate, 25-36 = moderately severe, above 36 = severe. Buprenorphine initiation is recommended at COWS 8-12 or above.

front: What is the role of quetiapine in bipolar disorder and what metabolic monitoring is required?
back: Quetiapine (Seroquel) is FDA-approved for bipolar mania, bipolar depression, and as adjunctive therapy in MDD. It is one of the few agents effective for both the manic and depressive phases of bipolar disorder. Metabolic monitoring includes fasting glucose, lipid panel, weight, BMI, and waist circumference at baseline, at 3 months, and then annually. Weight gain and metabolic syndrome are the most common significant adverse effects.

front: What is the difference between specific and social phobias, and how are they treated?
back: Specific phobias involve intense, irrational fear of a specific object or situation (animals, heights, blood, injections, flying) that is out of proportion to the actual danger. Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) specifically involves fear of negative evaluation in social situations. For specific phobias, exposure-based CBT (graduated exposure) is the primary treatment and is highly effective. Medications play a minimal role in specific phobia management, though benzodiazepines may be used short-term.

front: What is duloxetine (Cymbalta) and what conditions beyond depression is it approved to treat?
back: Duloxetine is an SNRI with FDA approvals for major depressive disorder, GAD, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia, and chronic musculoskeletal pain. The typical dose range is 30-120 mg daily. It is a moderate inhibitor of CYP2D6, which can raise levels of drugs metabolized by that enzyme, such as tricyclic antidepressants. Duloxetine should not be abruptly discontinued due to discontinuation syndrome.

front: What is antidepressant discontinuation syndrome and how is it managed?
back: Discontinuation syndrome occurs when SSRIs or SNRIs are abruptly stopped after regular use, presenting with flu-like symptoms, dizziness, insomnia, irritability, and electric shock sensations (brain zaps). Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the highest risk due to their short half-lives. Fluoxetine has the lowest risk due to its long half-life of 1-4 days (active metabolite 4-16 days). Management involves gradual tapering over weeks and, if needed, restarting the medication and tapering more slowly.

front: What medications are used for the acute management of mania in bipolar disorder?
back: Acute mania is managed with lithium (targeting a level of 0.8-1.2 mEq/L), valproate (targeting a level of 50-125 mcg/mL), or second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) such as olanzapine, quetiapine, or risperidone. Combination therapy (lithium or valproate plus an SGA) is often used for severe mania. Benzodiazepines may be added short-term for sedation and behavioral control. Antidepressants should be avoided during acute mania as they may trigger cycling.

front: What is the treatment for ADHD in patients with comorbid substance use disorder?
back: For patients with ADHD and comorbid substance use disorder (SUD), non-stimulant medications are preferred to reduce misuse risk. Atomoxetine (Strattera, 40-100 mg daily), bupropion (150-300 mg daily), and viloxazine (Qelbree) are first-line non-stimulant options. If stimulants are needed, long-acting formulations are preferred over short-acting ones. The SUD should be stabilized before initiating ADHD pharmacotherapy.

front: What is the clinical presentation of borderline personality disorder (BPD) and how is it managed?
back: BPD is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, affects, and marked impulsivity. DSM-5 requires 5 or more of 9 criteria including fear of abandonment, unstable relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity, suicidal or self-harming behavior, emotional instability, chronic emptiness, anger problems, and stress-related paranoia. The gold-standard treatment is dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). Medications target specific symptoms rather than the diagnosis itself.

front: What screening tool is used for alcohol misuse in primary care, and what scores indicate hazardous drinking?
back: The AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test) is the WHO-recommended 10-item tool for screening alcohol misuse in primary care settings. A score of 8-15 indicates hazardous or harmful drinking requiring brief counseling. A score of 16-19 indicates harmful drinking warranting brief counseling and monitoring. A score of 20 or above indicates likely dependence, requiring referral for further diagnostic evaluation and specialized treatment.

front: What is the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) used for in clinical practice?
back: The C-SSRS is a validated tool used to assess suicidal ideation and behavior in clinical and research settings. It measures the intensity of ideation (passive ideation, active ideation with or without plan or intent) and behavior (preparatory actions, interrupted attempts, aborted attempts, actual attempts). It helps standardize documentation and guide clinical decision-making about level of care. A patient with active suicidal ideation with a specific plan and intent requires inpatient evaluation.

front: What is the mechanism of buspirone and when is it used for anxiety?
back: Buspirone is a partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors and a weak dopamine D2 antagonist. It is used for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and has no addiction potential, making it a good option in patients with substance use disorder. The typical dose is 15-60 mg daily in divided doses (7.5-15 mg twice or three times daily). A major limitation is the delayed onset of 2-4 weeks, and it does not work for acute or as-needed anxiety relief.

front: What are the indications for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in psychiatric care?
back: ECT is indicated for severe, treatment-resistant MDD that has not responded to 2 or more adequate antidepressant trials, severe MDD with psychotic features, severe suicidality requiring rapid response, and catatonia unresponsive to benzodiazepines. ECT is also indicated in bipolar disorder with severe mania or depression, and in NMS. It has a response rate of approximately 70-90% in treatment-resistant depression, often within 2-3 weeks of treatment.

front: What are the cognitive effects of benzodiazepines in elderly patients, and what guideline addresses this?
back: Benzodiazepines in elderly patients significantly increase risks of sedation, cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, and hip fractures. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are particularly hazardous in the elderly due to prolonged half-lives. The American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria explicitly lists all benzodiazepines as potentially inappropriate in adults 65 and older. Non-pharmacologic approaches (sleep hygiene, CBT-I for insomnia) and shorter-acting alternatives should be prioritized.

front: What is the clinical presentation of delirium and how does it differ from dementia?
back: Delirium presents with acute onset (hours to days) of fluctuating altered attention, awareness, and cognition with an identifiable medical cause such as infection, medication toxicity, or metabolic disturbance. Key features are acute onset and fluctuating course. Dementia has an insidious onset over months to years with stable or slowly progressive course, and consciousness is preserved until late stages. The mnemonic DELIRIUM helps identify causes: Drugs, Electrolytes, Low O2, Infection, Retention (urinary/fecal), Ictal, Underhydration, Metabolic.

front: What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for insomnia disorder in adults?
back: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the gold-standard first-line treatment for chronic insomnia, more effective and more durable than medication. For pharmacologic treatment, FDA-approved options include doxepin 3-6 mg (for sleep maintenance), suvorexant (Belsomra, orexin receptor antagonist, 5-20 mg), and lemborexant. Zolpidem (Ambien) is commonly used but carries risks of dependence, parasomnia (sleepwalking), and cognitive impairment, particularly in women and older adults.

front: What is the difference between a hypomanic episode and a manic episode in bipolar spectrum disorders?
back: Hypomania lasts at least 4 consecutive days, does not require hospitalization, does not include psychotic features, and does not cause marked functional impairment. Mania lasts at least 7 days (or any duration requiring hospitalization), may include psychotic features, and causes marked functional impairment or necessitates inpatient care. Both require at least 3 additional DIGFAST symptoms: Distractibility, Impulsivity, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, and Talkativeness.

front: What is the risk of valproate in women of childbearing age with bipolar disorder?
back: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk among mood stabilizers and antiepileptic drugs. It causes neural tube defects (spina bifida) in approximately 1-2% of exposed pregnancies, and is also associated with cognitive impairment, autism spectrum features, and craniofacial abnormalities in children exposed in utero. Valproate should be avoided in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments have failed and reliable contraception is in place. Folic acid 4 mg daily should be taken if valproate cannot be avoided.

front: What are the symptoms of cannabis use disorder and how is it treated?
back: Cannabis use disorder is diagnosed when cannabis use leads to significant impairment including tolerance, withdrawal (irritability, sleep problems, decreased appetite, anxiety), using more than intended, failed attempts to quit, and continued use despite consequences. At least 2 of 11 criteria are required within 12 months. There are no FDA-approved medications for cannabis use disorder. CBT and motivational enhancement therapy are the most effective treatments. N-acetylcysteine has shown some benefit in adolescents.

front: What is adjustment disorder and how does it differ from MDD?
back: Adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioral reaction to an identifiable stressor occurring within 3 months of the stressor, that is out of proportion to the stressor's severity and causes significant impairment. Symptoms resolve within 6 months after the stressor ends. It does not meet full criteria for MDD, anxiety disorder, or PTSD. Treatment is primarily psychotherapy (supportive or CBT). Medications may be used short-term for specific symptoms such as sleep or anxiety, but are not the primary intervention.

front: What is the role of lithium in suicide prevention?
back: Lithium has the most robust evidence among all psychotropic medications for reducing suicide and suicidal behavior, with meta-analyses showing a 5-fold reduction in suicide risk in patients with bipolar disorder and MDD. The anti-suicidal effect appears independent of its mood-stabilizing properties and may be related to its effects on serotonin and impulsivity. This anti-suicidal effect is a major clinical reason to choose lithium over other mood stabilizers in high-risk patients.

front: What is the DAST-10 and what score warrants further assessment?
back: The DAST-10 (Drug Abuse Screening Test) is a validated 10-item questionnaire screening for problematic drug use (excluding alcohol and tobacco). Scores range from 0-10: 1-2 = low level, warrants monitoring; 3-5 = moderate level, warrants further assessment and intervention; 6-8 = substantial level, warrants assessment and referral; 9-10 = severe level, warrants immediate referral. It is widely used in primary care for annual substance use screening.

front: What is the recommended duration of antidepressant treatment after a first episode of MDD?
back: After achieving remission from a first episode of MDD, antidepressants should be continued for a minimum of 6-12 months before considering tapering, to prevent relapse. Patients with a history of 2 or more episodes, severe first episodes, or strong family history of MDD should be counseled about indefinite maintenance therapy. Tapering should be gradual over weeks to months, and the patient should be monitored closely for return of symptoms. Abrupt discontinuation significantly increases the relapse rate.

front: What is motivational interviewing (MI) and in what clinical situations is it most useful?
back: Motivational interviewing is a collaborative, patient-centered communication style designed to strengthen intrinsic motivation for behavior change by exploring and resolving ambivalence. It is most useful in managing substance use disorders, medication non-adherence, lifestyle changes for chronic disease (diabetes, obesity, hypertension), and smoking cessation. Core MI skills are summarized by OARS: Open-ended questions, Affirmations, Reflective listening, and Summaries. The provider avoids arguing or confronting the patient.

front: What are the clinical features that distinguish persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) from MDD?
back: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents), with at least 2 additional symptoms from: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and hopelessness. The depressed mood is less severe than MDD but more chronic. Patients may have symptom-free periods of no more than 2 months. Treatment includes SSRIs and psychotherapy.

front: What is the treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder when a patient has hypertension?
back: Stimulant medications (methylphenidate and amphetamine salts) can raise heart rate by 3-6 beats per minute and blood pressure by 2-4 mmHg, which is concerning in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. In patients with ADHD and hypertension, non-stimulant options such as atomoxetine, extended-release guanfacine (Intuniv 1-4 mg), or extended-release clonidine (Kapvay) are preferred. Guanfacine and clonidine are alpha-2 agonists that can actually lower blood pressure and address ADHD symptoms simultaneously.

front: What defines a psychotic disorder versus a mood disorder with psychotic features?
back: In a primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder), psychotic symptoms are the central feature and persist beyond mood episodes. In mood disorders with psychotic features (psychotic depression, mania with psychosis), psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during mood episodes and resolve when the mood episode resolves. Mood-congruent psychotic features (grandiose delusions in mania, nihilistic delusions in depression) are more common in mood disorders, while bizarre delusions and prominent negative symptoms suggest primary psychosis.

front: What is the pharmacologic treatment for generalized anxiety disorder in elderly patients?
back: In elderly patients with GAD, SSRIs (sertraline or escitalopram) and SNRIs (duloxetine) are preferred first-line pharmacologic options. Buspirone is also appropriate given its lack of dependence potential. Benzodiazepines should be avoided due to risks of falls, cognitive impairment, and delirium per the Beers Criteria. Pregabalin (75-300 mg daily) is an effective option, particularly for patients with comorbid pain. CBT adapted for older adults is effective and should be combined with medication.

front: What is the GAD-7 and how are scores interpreted?
back: The GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale) is a validated 7-item self-report screening and severity tool for GAD and anxiety in general. Scores of 5-9 indicate mild anxiety, 10-14 indicate moderate anxiety, and 15 or above indicate severe anxiety. A score of 10 or above is the standard threshold for further evaluation and treatment. The GAD-7 also screens for panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and PTSD, with a lower threshold of 8 used for these conditions.

front: What is the clinical presentation of conduct disorder versus oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) in children?
back: ODD is characterized by a persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, and vindictiveness toward authority figures, lasting 6 or more months. Conduct disorder (CD) is more severe and involves repetitive violation of others' rights or social rules, including aggression to people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, and serious rule violations. CD may progress to antisocial personality disorder in adulthood. Treatment for both includes parent management training and individual psychotherapy.

front: What are the CRAFFT screening questions and who should be screened?
back: The CRAFFT is a 6-item validated substance use screening tool for adolescents ages 12-21 used in primary care. Questions ask: Car (ridden with someone high), Relax (used to relax), Alone (used alone), Forget (forgotten things while using), Friends/Family (told you should cut down), Trouble (gotten into trouble while using). A score of 2 or more indicates high-risk use warranting brief intervention and possible referral. The AAP recommends annual CRAFFT screening at all adolescent well visits.

front: What is the mechanism and clinical use of lamotrigine in bipolar disorder?
back: Lamotrigine (Lamictal) stabilizes neuronal membranes by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels and inhibiting glutamate release. It is FDA-approved for the maintenance treatment of Bipolar I disorder and is the preferred agent for the depressive phase of Bipolar II. It is generally weight-neutral and does not cause cognitive dulling. The major adverse effect is Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), which is avoided by starting at 25 mg daily and titrating slowly over 6-8 weeks. Concurrent valproate doubles lamotrigine levels, requiring starting at 12.5 mg every other day.

front: What is the screening tool for PTSD in primary care, and what score indicates a positive screen?
back: The PC-PTSD-5 (Primary Care PTSD Screen for DSM-5) is a validated 5-item tool recommended for PTSD screening in primary care. A score of 3 or more (answering yes to 3 of 5 questions about nightmares, avoidance, on guard, feeling numb, and guilt/blame) is a positive screen requiring further evaluation. The PCL-5 (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5) is a 20-item tool used to assess PTSD symptom severity, with a score of 31-33 or above suggesting likely PTSD diagnosis.

front: What is harm reduction in the context of substance use disorders, and what are examples of harm reduction strategies?
back: Harm reduction is a public health approach that aims to minimize the negative health, social, and economic consequences of substance use without requiring abstinence as a precondition for services. Examples include needle exchange programs (reducing HIV/HCV transmission), naloxone distribution to people who use opioids (reversing overdose), fentanyl test strips, supervised consumption sites, and providing clean smoking supplies. Medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine, methadone) is itself considered a harm reduction strategy.

front: What is the difference between opioid tolerance, physical dependence, and addiction?
back: Tolerance is a physiologic adaptation where the same dose produces less effect over time, requiring dose increases for the same result. Physical dependence is a physiologic state where abrupt discontinuation produces withdrawal symptoms; it occurs with any regular opioid use and does not indicate addiction. Opioid use disorder (addiction) involves compulsive use despite negative consequences, loss of control, and craving. Patients with cancer pain on opioids may be tolerant and physically dependent without having OUD.

front: What are the diagnostic features of somatic symptom disorder (SSD)?
back: Somatic symptom disorder (SSD) requires one or more somatic symptoms causing significant distress or functional impairment, plus excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to those symptoms for at least 6 months. The symptoms may or may not have a clear medical explanation; the diagnosis is not one of exclusion. SSD replaces DSM-IV diagnoses of somatization disorder, hypochondriasis, and undifferentiated somatoform disorder. First-line treatment is CBT and regularly scheduled primary care visits, avoiding reactive testing and referrals.

front: What is the first-line treatment for tobacco use disorder (nicotine dependence)?
back: The most effective treatment for tobacco cessation is combination pharmacotherapy plus behavioral counseling. Varenicline (Chantix, 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks) is the most effective single agent. Combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus lozenge or gum) is also highly effective. Bupropion 150 mg twice daily is a second-line agent. All patients who smoke should be counseled using the 5 A's: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange follow-up.

front: What are the features of narcissistic personality disorder and how does it present in clinical encounters?
back: Narcissistic personality disorder (NPD) is characterized by a pervasive pattern of grandiosity, need for admiration, and lack of empathy, with 5 or more of 9 DSM-5 criteria including grandiose sense of self-importance, preoccupation with fantasies of unlimited success, sense of entitlement, interpersonal exploitation, and arrogant behaviors. In clinical encounters, patients may be dismissive of providers, demand special treatment, or become angry when given unfavorable diagnoses. Psychotherapy, particularly transference-focused therapy, is the primary treatment.

front: What is the pharmacologic management of acute alcohol withdrawal requiring hospitalization?
back: Hospitalized patients with alcohol withdrawal are managed with symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocols guided by CIWA-Ar scores. Long-acting benzodiazepines such as diazepam (5-20 mg IV/PO q1-2h PRN) are preferred for self-tapering via redistribution. In patients with liver disease, lorazepam (1-2 mg q4-6h) or oxazepam (which avoid hepatic metabolism) are preferred.
